During the annealing process, stored energy release drives recrystallization nucleation and grain growth.

Annealing at 600 ◦ C induces grain growth and recrystallization, reducing internal stress and dislocation density. This facilitates more extensive dislocation multiplication and slip during tensile testing, enhancing material plasticity.
Cold rolling elongated these grains into a fibrous morphology and generates a high density of parallel dislocations, signifying severe work hardening.

Conversely, when temperature increased from 800 ◦ C to 900 ◦ C, the driving force for recrystallization diminishes, grain coarsening ensues, and grains with relatively high SF obtain a size advantage, causing the average SF to fall slightly back to 0.44.
